passage:
Session note, Avni, campus career counsellor.

Jomon, aged 24, asked to see me after a friend posted a photo beside a new car, with screenshots of trading profits. Jomon said, "Everyone my age is ahead." Sleep had been poor for a week, and a trading account had been opened the night before but not yet funded.

I asked what the friend's posts leave out. Jomon thought for a while: losses, months of waiting, maybe borrowed money. I asked Jomon to write down a plan for the next year: savings, a certification, a small emergency fund. Jomon looked at the list and said, "It looks slow next to a car." I said slow is allowed.

Jomon agreed to read about how such accounts work before putting in any money. We meet again next month.

qa.q: What did the friend post that upset Jomon?
qa.a: The friend posted a photo beside a new car, with screenshots of trading profits.

qa.q: What does Jomon's remark "Everyone my age is ahead" suggest about Jomon's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Jomon feels left behind and envious, and the poor sleep for a week points to how much it weighs.

qa.q: What small step would help Jomon compare fairly?
qa.a: Compare against the written plan of savings, a certification and an emergency fund, and learn how trading accounts work before putting in money.

qa.q: How might the friend see those posts?
qa.a: The friend may simply be sharing a win without thinking how it lands on Jomon, and the posts leave out losses and waiting that Jomon guessed at.

grounding: A friend flaunts trading profits and Jomon feels left behind; the counsellor helps Jomon compare with their own plan instead of highlights.

passage: Nitin, you keep looking at your friend's photos with his new car. I know that face. At your age, twenty-five, I was a young woman working at a publishing house in Delhi, and my college friend Rima started posting about her share-trading profits. New phone. Holiday in Goa. A car in the second year. I felt left behind, like a fool with my steady salary. One evening I nearly moved all my savings into the same thing she was doing, which I didn't understand at all. My mother asked, "Has she ever shown you her losses?" I realised I'd only seen the wins. Later I learned Rima had lost a lot in the crash and never posted it. I stuck to my own plan and asked a registered adviser before doing anything I didn't understand. It was boring. It worked. That's what Ishita-maasi has to tell you, Nitin.

qa.q: What did Rima buy in the second year?
What was Ishita feeling while watching Rima's posts?
qa.a: She felt envious and left behind, like a fool with her steady salary.

qa.q: What turning point in the story stopped Ishita from rushing in?
qa.a: Her mother's question about Rima's losses made her see she had only seen the wins, so she stuck to her own plan and asked a registered adviser.

qa.q: How might Rima have felt when her losses came?
qa.a: Rima was probably stressed and embarrassed, which is why she never posted about them.

grounding: An elder recalls envying a friend's trading profits, realising social media shows only wins, and sticking to her own plan with a registered adviser.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded Kiran's street in Chennai, and he was stuck at home for the third day, scrolling. Suraj, his friend from college, had posted again: a new SUV, a screenshot of "today's trading profit", a caption about quitting the nine-to-five.
Kiran looked at his own salary slip on the table and felt his stomach sink. He'd been saving steadily for two years. It suddenly felt pathetic.
He opened the trading app Suraj had shared. The sign-up bonus countdown said: 2 hours left. He didn't understand options trading, but maybe he could learn on the way?
His thumb hovered. Then he closed the app and called his elder sister, who worked as a financial planner. "Suraj posts his wins," she said. "Has he ever posted a loss?" Kiran scrolled. Not once.
He switched off the phone, made tea, and opened his own savings plan instead.

qa.q: How long did the sign-up bonus countdown say was left?
What was Kiran feeling as he looked at his salary slip?
qa.a: He felt envious and left behind, his stomach sinking, as if his steady saving were pathetic.

qa.q: What did Kiran do instead of rushing into options trading?
qa.a: He closed the app, called his sister who is a financial planner, noticed Suraj only posted wins, and returned to his own savings plan.

qa.q: How might Suraj's posts look different if they showed everything?
qa.a: If Suraj posted losses too, Kiran would likely see a riskier picture and feel less pressure to copy him.

grounding: A friend flaunts trading profits and a new car; the protagonist feels left behind but sees the posts show only wins and sticks to his own plan.
